source_text:
Angus Taylor has drawn a clear line against Andrew Hastie’s proposal to consider higher taxes on gas companies and reducing concessions for property investors. That is more than a policy disagreement: it exposes a contest over whether the Liberals will back investment and economic stability or flirt with tax changes that could undermine them.

Hastie’s criticism of Donald Trump and Taylor’s refusal to say whether he supports the US and Israel’s war with Iran add to the impression of a party struggling to settle on a consistent direction. Voters need clarity and responsible leadership, not a public contest over who may lead next.
rewritten_text:
Taylor is right to draw a line against higher taxes on gas companies and cuts to property-investor concessions. Treating investment as a cash cow may play well with people who want government to solve everything, but it risks undermining economic stability and the confidence families and businesses depend on.

Hastie’s criticism of Trump and Taylor’s refusal to say whether he supports the US and Israel’s war with Iran only deepen the impression of a party arguing over its direction in public. Conservatives should be able to debate policy, but voters need a united, responsible leadership—not a contest over who gets to lead next or uncertainty when serious international issues demand clarity.

The opposition leader also did not repeat Hastie’s criticism of Donald Trump as he refused to say whether or not he endorsed the US and Israel’s war with Iran. Continue reading...

source_text:
Taylor is right to draw a line against higher taxes on gas companies and cuts to property-investor concessions. Treating investment as a cash cow may play well with people who want government to solve everything, but it risks undermining economic stability and the confidence families and businesses depend on.

Hastie’s criticism of Trump and Taylor’s refusal to say whether he supports the US and Israel’s war with Iran only deepen the impression of a party arguing over its direction in public. Conservatives should be able to debate policy, but voters need a united, responsible leadership—not a contest over who gets to lead next or uncertainty when serious international issues demand clarity.
rewritten_text:

But conservatives also need discipline and clear leadership. Hastie’s criticism of Trump, alongside Taylor’s refusal to say whether he supports the US and Israel’s war with Iran, makes the party look more interested in an internal leadership contest than in giving voters a responsible direction. Debate is healthy, but when serious international issues arise, the public deserves a clear account of where its leaders stand and how they will put the national interest first.

source_text:
Taylor is right to resist higher taxes on gas companies and cuts to property-investor concessions. Government should not treat investment as an endless source of revenue; stable rules matter to families and businesses, and economic confidence is part of the foundation of a secure society.

But conservatives also need discipline and clear leadership. Hastie’s criticism of Trump, alongside Taylor’s refusal to say whether he supports the US and Israel’s war with Iran, makes the party look more interested in an internal leadership contest than in giving voters a responsible direction. Debate is healthy, but when serious international issues arise, the public deserves a clear account of where its leaders stand and how they will put the national interest first.

Stable rules and personal responsibility matter; government cannot promise security while constantly shifting the terms for those who invest and build.

Hastie’s criticism of Trump and Taylor’s refusal to say where he stands on the US and Israel’s war with Iran leave voters watching an internal contest instead of hearing clear leadership. On matters of national interest, evasion is not prudence. The party needs discipline, a plain account of its position, and leaders prepared to put the country first.
